fact_text: The H-1B nonimmigrant classification is subject to a numerical cap of 65,000 visas per fiscal year. An additional 20,000 H-1B petitions are exempt from the cap for beneficiaries who hold a U.S. master's degree or higher from a U.S. institution of higher education. When petitions exceed available numbers, USCIS conducts a computer-generated random lottery.
evidence_quote: The H-1B program allows employers to temporarily employ foreign workers in the United States on a nonimmigrant basis in specialty occupations. The number of H-1B workers that may be approved is limited by statute: 65,000 for the general cap, plus an additional 20,000 for those who have earned a master's degree or higher from a U.S. institution.

fact_text: A specialty occupation requires the theoretical and practical application of a body of highly specialized knowledge and the attainment of a bachelor's or higher degree in the specific specialty (or its equivalent) as a minimum for entry into the occupation in the United States.
evidence_quote: Specialty occupation means an occupation that requires theoretical and practical application of a body of highly specialized knowledge and attainment of a bachelor's or higher degree in the specific specialty (or its equivalent) as a minimum for entry into the occupation in the United States.

fact_text: Before filing Form I-129 (Petition for Nonimmigrant Worker) with USCIS, the employer must obtain a certified Labor Condition Application (LCA) from the Department of Labor. The LCA is filed electronically through the DOL's FLAG system and attests to wage and working conditions.
evidence_quote: Before filing a petition with USCIS, the employer must file a Labor Condition Application (LCA), Form ETA 9035/9035E, electronically with the Department of Labor. The LCA must be certified before the I-129 petition is submitted to USCIS.

fact_text: The LCA effective date may not be more than 6 months before the start of the employment period on the H-1B petition. The LCA must be valid at the time the H-1B petition is filed with USCIS.
evidence_quote: The beginning date of employment shown on the LCA shall be no more than 6 months before the start date of H-1B employment.

fact_text: DOL is required to review and either certify or reject the LCA within 7 working days of submission, unless the application is incomplete or contains obvious inaccuracies.
evidence_quote: The Department will review and either certify or reject the LCA within 7 working days of submission. If the Department fails to act within 7 working days, the LCA will be deemed certified.

fact_text: Employers must pay H-1B workers the higher of the actual wage paid to similarly situated employees at the employer's worksite, or the prevailing wage for the occupational classification in the area of intended employment. The prevailing wage is determined by the National Prevailing Wage Center (NPWC) or an independent authoritative source.
evidence_quote: The employer must pay the H-1B worker the higher of the actual wage or the prevailing wage for the occupational classification in the area of intended employment.

fact_text: Form I-129 (Petition for Nonimmigrant Worker) is the petition form filed by the employer with USCIS to request H-1B classification. The H-1B supplement must be included. The petition must be accompanied by the certified LCA, degree documentation, and employer support documentation.
evidence_quote: The employer files Form I-129, Petition for Nonimmigrant Worker, with USCIS. The petition includes the certified LCA, the H Classification Supplement, and supporting documentation demonstrating the position qualifies as a specialty occupation and the alien meets the requirements.

fact_text: H-1B petitions are subject to additional fees beyond the base I-129 filing fee: (1) $500 Fraud Prevention and Detection Fee for initial petitions and employer changes; (2) $1,500 ACWIA Training Fee for employers with >25 full-time employees ($750 for ≤25 FTE); (3) $4,000 additional fee for certain employers with 50+ employees if more than 50% are in H-1B or L-1 status (Public Law 114-113).
evidence_quote: H-1B petitions require: $500 fraud prevention fee; ACWIA training fee of $1,500 (if more than 25 full-time equivalent employees) or $750 (if 25 or fewer); and in some cases an additional fee under P.L. 114-113 for employers with 50+ employees if more than 50 percent are in H-1B or L-1 nonimmigrant status.

fact_text: To apply for an F-1 student visa and to be admitted to the US in F-1 status, a student must have a valid Form I-20 (Certificate of Eligibility for Nonimmigrant Student Status) issued by a SEVP-certified school. The I-20 is generated in SEVIS and signed by a Designated School Official (DSO).
evidence_quote: The Form I-20 is a federal document that the DSO creates in SEVIS to certify that a student has been admitted to a full course of study at that school and that the student has adequate financial resources. You must have an I-20 to apply for an F-1 or M-1 student visa at a U.S. Embassy or Consulate.

fact_text: F-1 and M-1 students must pay the SEVIS I-901 fee of $350 before applying for a student visa at a U.S. consulate or before entering the US. Payment is made through FMJfee.com. The fee applies to each new SEVIS record.
evidence_quote: Students must pay the SEVIS fee (I-901 fee) of $350 for F-1 and M-1 students ($220 for J-1 exchange visitors) before applying for a visa or entering the United States. Payment is made at FMJfee.com.

fact_text: F-1 students may enter the US no earlier than 30 days before the program start date listed on their I-20. Attempting to enter the US more than 30 days before the program start date will result in denial of admission.
evidence_quote: You can be admitted up to 30 days before the program start date on your Form I-20. If you try to enter the United States more than 30 days before that date, you will be refused admission.

fact_text: F-1 students must present their signed Form I-20 to CBP officers at the US port of entry. The I-20 is reviewed as part of the admission process and must be valid and signed by both the DSO and the student.
evidence_quote: Always carry your current Form I-20 because you will need it when you travel, apply for a driver's license, and for other official purposes. You must present your signed I-20 to the CBP officer at the port of entry.

fact_text: F-2 dependents (spouse and children) of F-1 students each require their own Form I-20 listing them as dependents. The primary F-1 student's DSO creates dependent I-20s in SEVIS. F-2 dependents must also pay the SEVIS I-901 fee ($35 for F-2 dependents).
evidence_quote: F-2 dependents need their own Form I-20 documents. Your DSO will create dependent I-20s for your spouse and children in SEVIS. Each dependent pays a separate, reduced SEVIS fee.

fact_text: J-1 exchange visitors must pay the SEVIS I-901 fee of $220 before applying for a visa or entering the US. Certain government-sponsored and fully government-funded exchange visitors may be exempt. Payment is made at FMJfee.com.
evidence_quote: J-1 exchange visitors pay the SEVIS fee of $220. Government-sponsored exchange visitors may be exempt from this fee.

fact_text: F-1 students who have been lawfully enrolled full-time for one full academic year are eligible for Optional Practical Training (OPT) in a job directly related to their major area of study. OPT may be used before graduation (pre-completion) or after (post-completion). Total OPT period: 12 months. Each degree level grants a new 12-month OPT period.
evidence_quote: Optional Practical Training (OPT) is temporary employment that is directly related to an F-1 student's major area of study. Eligible students can apply to receive up to 12 months of OPT employment authorization before completing their academic studies (pre-completion) and/or after completing their academic studies (post-completion).

fact_text: To obtain OPT work authorization, the F-1 student must apply for an Employment Authorization Document (EAD) by filing Form I-765 with USCIS. The DSO must first recommend OPT in SEVIS. The student should apply 90 days before the intended OPT start date but no earlier than 90 days before the end of the program.
evidence_quote: Once your DSO has recommended OPT in SEVIS, you must file Form I-765, Application for Employment Authorization, with USCIS. You can apply up to 90 days before your program end date, but no later than 60 days after your program ends for post-completion OPT.

fact_text: F-1 students who have earned a degree in a STEM field (as listed on the STEM Designated Degree Program List) from a SEVP-certified institution may apply for a 24-month STEM OPT extension, bringing total OPT to 36 months. The employer must be enrolled in E-Verify.
evidence_quote: The STEM OPT extension is a 24-month period of OPT that an F-1 student with a STEM degree may be eligible to apply for. To be eligible, the student's degree must be included on the STEM Designated Degree Program List, and the employer must be enrolled in and using E-Verify.

fact_text: For STEM OPT, the employer and student must complete Form I-983 (Training Plan for STEM OPT Students) describing the practical training the employer will provide. The training plan must detail goals, objectives, and how the training relates to the student's STEM degree. The employer must be E-Verify enrolled.
evidence_quote: Form I-983, Training Plan for STEM OPT Students, must be completed and signed by both the student and the employer. The training plan details the specific goals, objectives, and coursework tied to the STEM OPT experience. The employer must be enrolled in E-Verify.

fact_text: Curricular Practical Training (CPT) is an alternative work/study, internship, cooperative education, or any other type of required internship or practicum that is offered by sponsoring employers through cooperative agreements with the school. CPT must be an integral part of an established curriculum and must be authorized by the DSO before the student begins working.
evidence_quote: Curricular Practical Training (CPT) is an alternative work/study, internship, cooperative education, or any other type of required internship or practicum that is offered by sponsoring employers through cooperative agreements with the school. CPT is integral to the student's established curriculum.

fact_text: To qualify for L-1A classification, the employee must have been employed by the petitioning employer or a qualifying organization (affiliate, subsidiary, or parent) outside the United States in an executive or managerial capacity for a continuous period of at least one year within the three years immediately preceding the filing of the petition.
evidence_quote: To qualify for L-1A classification, the employer must file a petition on behalf of an employee who has been employed by a qualifying organization outside the U.S. for one continuous year within the three years immediately preceding the petition filing in a managerial or executive capacity, and seeks to enter the U.S. to provide service in a managerial or executive capacity.

fact_text: L-1A beneficiaries are initially admitted for 3 years (or 1 year if coming to open a new US office). Extensions may be granted in increments of 2 years. The maximum period of stay is 7 years for L-1A. Time spent in L-1B status counts toward the 7-year maximum for L-1B (5-year cap).
evidence_quote: L-1A nonimmigrants admitted to the United States to establish a new office may be admitted for a period not to exceed 1 year. All other L-1A nonimmigrants may be admitted for up to 3 years. For all L-1A nonimmigrants, requests for extension of stay may be granted in increments of up to 2 years, until the individual has reached the maximum limit of 7 years.

fact_text: Qualifying organizations may file a blanket L petition to streamline the transfer of many employees. Once a blanket petition is approved, individual employees may apply directly at a U.S. consulate for an L-1 visa using Form I-129S instead of requiring a separate I-129 petition for each employee.
evidence_quote: As an alternative to an individual L petition, qualifying organizations may file a blanket petition. Once a blanket petition is approved, employees covered under the blanket petition may apply directly for L-1 visa status at a U.S. consulate abroad without the employer needing to file individual I-129 petitions.

fact_text: As of November 12, 2021, L-2 nonimmigrant spouses have work authorization incident to their status. L-2 spouses may work based on their I-94 admission record without filing a separate I-765 for an EAD. CBP issues I-94 records endorsing L-2 work authorization. L-2 children do not have automatic work authorization.
evidence_quote: Effective November 12, 2021, USCIS considers L-2 nonimmigrant spouses to be employment authorized incident to status. L-2 spouses may present their unexpired I-94 as a List A document for Form I-9 employment eligibility verification purposes.

fact_text: O-1A classification requires extraordinary ability in the sciences, education, business, or athletics, demonstrated by sustained national or international acclaim. The standard is met by evidence of a major internationally recognized award (such as a Nobel Prize) OR at least 3 of 8 evidentiary criteria: prizes/awards, membership requiring outstanding achievement, press/media coverage, judging others' work, original contributions of major significance, scholarly articles, critical role in distinguished organizations, or high salary.
evidence_quote: To qualify for O-1A classification, the beneficiary must demonstrate extraordinary ability in the sciences, education, business, or athletics by sustained national or international acclaim and recognition. Evidence includes a major internationally recognized award, or at least three of the following: nationally or internationally recognized prizes or awards; membership in associations requiring outstanding achievement; published material about the beneficiary; judging the work of others; original contributions of major significance; authorship of scholarly articles; displayed at artistic exhibitions; performed in a leading or critical role; high salary; and commercial successes in the performing arts.

fact_text: The O-1 visa category has no annual numerical cap. O-1 petitions may be filed and approved at any time of year. This distinguishes O-1 from H-1B, which is subject to an annual cap and lottery when oversubscribed.
evidence_quote: Unlike the H-1B category, the O-1 nonimmigrant category is not subject to a numerical cap. O-1 petitions can be filed and adjudicated at any time during the year.

fact_text: For O-1A petitions, USCIS requires the petitioner to submit a written advisory opinion from a peer group (labor organization or management organization) or a person with expertise in the field, attesting to the beneficiary's extraordinary ability. If no appropriate peer group exists, USCIS may accept a letter from an expert.
evidence_quote: Petitioners must consult with an appropriate peer group, labor organization, or person with expertise in the beneficiary's field and submit a written advisory opinion. For O-1A (sciences, education, business, athletics), the advisory opinion is required from an appropriate labor organization or peer group.

fact_text: O-3 nonimmigrants (spouses and children of O-1 holders) are not authorized to work in the United States. They may attend school full-time. There is no O-3 EAD category analogous to H-4 EAD or J-2 EAD.
evidence_quote: O-3 nonimmigrant spouses and unmarried minor children of O-1 nonimmigrants are not authorized to work in the United States. They may, however, attend school on a full-time basis.

fact_text: EB-1A (Aliens of Extraordinary Ability) is the only employment-based green card category that allows self-petition — no employer or labor certification is required. The beneficiary must demonstrate extraordinary ability in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics by sustained national or international acclaim. The beneficiary must also demonstrate they will continue to work in the area of extraordinary ability.
evidence_quote: Aliens of extraordinary ability in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics can self-petition for EB-1A classification. No job offer or labor certification is needed. You must demonstrate sustained national or international acclaim and that your achievements have been recognized in the field through extensive documentation.

fact_text: EB-1C (Multinational Managers and Executives) requires that the beneficiary has been employed outside the US for at least 1 year within the 3 preceding years in an executive or managerial capacity for the same employer (or qualifying affiliate) now petitioning in the US. A common pathway is L-1A → EB-1C. No PERM required.
evidence_quote: EB-1C is available to multinational executives and managers who have been employed outside the United States for at least one year in the three years preceding the petition in an executive or managerial capacity, and who will be employed in the United States in a managerial or executive capacity. No labor certification is required.

fact_text: EB-2 National Interest Waiver (NIW) allows qualified individuals to self-petition for an EB-2 green card without employer sponsorship or PERM labor certification. The petitioner must show: (1) the proposed work has substantial merit and national importance; (2) the petitioner is well-positioned to advance the proposed endeavor; (3) on balance, it would be beneficial to the US to waive the job offer and labor certification requirements.
evidence_quote: An EB-2 National Interest Waiver petition requires the petitioner to demonstrate that: (1) the proposed endeavor has both substantial merit and national importance; (2) the petitioner is well positioned to advance the proposed endeavor; and (3) on balance, it would be beneficial to the United States to waive the requirements of a job offer and thus a labor certification.

fact_text: EB-3 includes three subcategories: (1) Skilled Workers — at least 2 years of training or experience, not of a temporary or seasonal nature; (2) Professionals — bachelor's degree or foreign equivalent; (3) Other Workers — unskilled labor requiring less than 2 years training or experience. All EB-3 subcategories require an approved PERM labor certification.
evidence_quote: Third preference (EB-3) includes skilled workers (requiring at least two years of training or experience), professionals (requiring a U.S. bachelor's degree or foreign equivalent), and other workers (unskilled labor requiring less than two years training). All EB-3 subcategories require a PERM labor certification from the Department of Labor.

fact_text: PERM labor certification requires the employer to conduct supervised recruitment (job advertisements) to demonstrate that no qualified US workers are available for the position. Recruitment must include at least 3 additional steps beyond the mandatory Sunday newspaper advertisement. DOL reviews ETA Form 9089 and may audit. Current PERM processing: 6-18 months.
evidence_quote: The employer must conduct recruitment (supervised by DOL standards) to demonstrate there are no able, willing, qualified, and available U.S. workers for the position. Recruitment includes mandatory steps such as a Sunday newspaper advertisement and at least three additional steps from a prescribed list. The employer then files ETA Form 9089 with DOL.

fact_text: Upon approval of Form I-140, the beneficiary's priority date is established as the date the PERM application was filed with DOL (or the I-140 filing date for categories not requiring PERM). The priority date is retained even if the employer withdraws the I-140, as long as the I-140 was approved and not revoked for fraud or misrepresentation (AC21 protection after 6+ months).
evidence_quote: When you file an I-140 petition based on an approved PERM, the priority date is the date the PERM labor certification application was filed with the DOL. Once an I-140 petition is approved, the priority date is generally retained even if the petitioner withdraws the petition, under AC21 protections applicable after 180 days.

fact_text: The H-1B petition (Form I-129) must be filed by the employer (petitioner) on behalf of the worker (beneficiary). The worker cannot self-petition for H-1B status. The employer must maintain the petitioner relationship and is responsible for paying the worker's return transportation if the worker is dismissed before the end of the authorized period.
evidence_quote: The H-1B nonimmigrant petition must be filed by the employer, not the worker. The employer is the petitioner and files Form I-129 on behalf of the alien beneficiary. The worker cannot self-petition for H-1B classification.

fact_text: Canadian TN applicants apply directly at the US port of entry and are admitted on the spot — no advance visa or petition filing required. Mexican TN applicants must obtain a TN visa stamp at a US consulate before seeking admission. Both Canadian and Mexican TN workers must present a letter from the employer and evidence of their qualifying profession.
evidence_quote: Canadian citizens may apply for TN status at a U.S. port of entry. They do not need a visa to apply for TN status. Mexican citizens must apply for TN visas at a U.S. Embassy or Consulate before seeking admission to the United States.

fact_text: The TN category has no annual numerical cap and does not require an employer to file a Form I-129 petition (unlike H-1B). The admission decision is made by CBP at the port of entry (for Canadians) or at the consular post (for Mexicans). TN is granted in 3-year increments, renewable indefinitely.
evidence_quote: There is no annual cap on TN nonimmigrant status and no requirement for the employer to file a petition with USCIS before the alien can seek TN status. TN status is approved in 3-year increments and may be renewed indefinitely.

fact_text: O-1 nonimmigrants are initially admitted for up to 3 years and the period of event or activity, whichever is shorter. Extensions may be granted in 1-year increments. There is no maximum length of stay for O-1 status, distinguishing it from L-1 (7-year max) and H-1B (6-year max).
evidence_quote: An O-1 nonimmigrant may be admitted for a period of up to 3 years. After that, the O-1 nonimmigrant may receive extensions of stay in 1-year increments. There is no maximum limit on the total period of stay for O-1 nonimmigrants.

fact_text: Effective September 15, 2026, DHS replaced the Duration of Status (D/S) admission practice for F, M, and J nonimmigrants with fixed Admit Until Dates (AUD). Students admitted on or after September 15, 2026 will receive a specific end date on their I-94 rather than D/S. Students must file for an Extension of Stay (EOS) before their AUD expires if their program continues beyond that date. DHS rule: 2026-14439, published July 17, 2026.
evidence_quote: DHS has published a final rule (2026-14439) to replace Duration of Status admission practices for F, M, and J nonimmigrants with fixed Admit Until Dates (AUD), effective September 15, 2026. Students admitted on or after this date will receive a specific end date on their Form I-94 rather than 'D/S.' If a student's program extends beyond their AUD, they must file a timely application for extension of stay.

fact_text: H-1B1 is a specialty occupation nonimmigrant status available exclusively to Chilean nationals (annual cap: 1,400) and Singaporean nationals (annual cap: 5,400) under their respective free trade agreements with the US. The H-1B1 cap is separate from the regular H-1B cap. H-1B1 holders' spouses are not eligible for work authorization (unlike H-4 EAD).
evidence_quote: The H-1B1 nonimmigrant category is available to nationals of Chile (capped at 1,400 per year) and Singapore (capped at 5,400 per year) under free trade agreements. H-1B1 visas are issued at U.S. consulates. The H-1B1 cap is separate from the H-1B cap. Spouses of H-1B1 workers do not have work authorization.

fact_text: H-4 spouses of H-1B holders are eligible to apply for employment authorization (H-4 EAD) if the principal H-1B holder has an approved Form I-140, OR if the H-1B holder has been granted an extension of status beyond the 6-year maximum under AC21 (7th year or beyond). Eligibility is not automatic — the H-4 spouse must file Form I-765 to obtain the EAD.
evidence_quote: An H-4 dependent spouse of an H-1B nonimmigrant may apply for employment authorization if the H-1B principal's Form I-140 has been approved, or if the H-1B principal has been granted an H-1B extension of stay beyond the 6-year cap under INA 106(a) or (b). The H-4 spouse must file Form I-765 to obtain EAD.

fact_text: To obtain H-4 EAD, the H-4 spouse files Form I-765 (Application for Employment Authorization) with USCIS, category (c)(26). The petition must be accompanied by evidence of the principal's I-140 approval or AC21 extension, and the H-4 spouse's status documentation. Processing typically takes 6 to 16.5 months as of 2025-2026.
evidence_quote: H-4 EAD applicants file Form I-765 under category (c)(26). The H-4 spouse must provide evidence that the H-1B principal has an approved I-140 or is in 7th-year H-1B status. Current Form I-765 processing times range from 6 to 16.5 months.

fact_text: As of October 30, 2025, H-4 EAD renewals no longer qualify for the 180-day automatic extension that previously allowed H-4 EAD holders to continue working while a renewal application was pending. H-4 EAD renewal applications filed on or after October 30, 2025 must be approved before the prior EAD expires to maintain work authorization. Indian H-4 spouses face work-authorization gaps of 6-16.5 months during renewal processing.
evidence_quote: Effective October 30, 2025, H-4 EAD categories are no longer eligible for the 180-day automatic extension under the cap-subject H-1B or AC21 rule. H-4 EAD holders whose EADs expire while a renewal application is pending will experience a gap in employment authorization during that period.

fact_text: The J-1 Exchange Visitor Program has 16 BridgeUSA categories designated by the U.S. Department of State: student (college/university), student (secondary), short-term scholar, research scholar, professor, specialist, alien physician, international visitor, government visitor, camp counselor, au pair, summer work travel, teacher, trainee, intern, and border commuter student.
evidence_quote: The Exchange Visitor Program offers 16 BridgeUSA program categories. Each category requires sponsorship by a designated program sponsor authorized by the Department of State. Categories include: student (college/university), student (secondary), short-term scholar, research scholar, professor, specialist, alien physician, international visitor, government visitor, camp counselor, au pair, summer work travel, teacher, trainee, intern, and border commuter student.

fact_text: J-1 exchange visitors must have a Form DS-2019 (Certificate of Eligibility for Exchange Visitor Status), issued by a State Department-designated program sponsor. The DS-2019 is required to apply for a J-1 visa and to enter the US in J-1 status. It must be signed by the Responsible Officer (RO) of the sponsoring organization.
evidence_quote: All J-1 exchange visitors must receive a Form DS-2019 from their designated J-1 sponsor organization before applying for a J visa at a U.S. consulate or entering the United States. The DS-2019 is the Certificate of Eligibility for Exchange Visitor Status and must be signed by the Responsible Officer.

fact_text: Certain J-1 exchange visitors are subject to a two-year foreign residence requirement (INA § 212(e)) and must return to their home country for 2 years before being eligible to apply for H, L, or K nonimmigrant status or for an immigrant visa. The requirement applies when the exchange program was financed by the US government, the home country government, or when the J-1's skills are on the Exchange Visitor Skills List.
evidence_quote: Some J-1 exchange visitors are subject to the two-year home-country physical presence requirement under INA 212(e). This requirement applies if: (1) the exchange program was financed by the U.S. or the participant's home country government; (2) the participant's skills are in short supply in their home country (the Exchange Visitor Skills List); or (3) the participant came to the U.S. to receive graduate medical training. J-1 participants subject to this requirement must return to their home country for 2 years before they can change status to H or L or apply for an immigrant visa.

fact_text: J-2 nonimmigrant spouses and minor children of J-1 exchange visitors may apply for employment authorization by filing Form I-765 with USCIS under category (c)(5). Employment authorization is not automatic. J-2 employment income may not be used to support the J-1 principal. Authorization may be granted for up to 4 years or the duration of the J-1 program, whichever is shorter. Regulatory basis: 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(5).
evidence_quote: 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(5): 'An alien spouse or minor child of an exchange visitor (J-2) pursuant to § 214.2(j) of this chapter.' USCIS Policy Manual (Vol. 2, Part D, Ch. 6): 'J-2 nonimmigrants may be eligible for employment authorization; however, they may not use their income to support the J-1 nonimmigrant. To apply for employment authorization as a J-2 nonimmigrant, the dependent family member must file an Application for Employment Authorization (Form I-765). USCIS may authorize the employment for the length of the J-1 exchange visitor's stay or 4 years, whichever is shorter.'
note: Upgraded from LOW to HIGH in Batch 3 (US-B3-006) with verbatim regulatory citation.

fact_text: Effective September 15, 2026, DHS eliminated the Duration of Status (D/S) admission practice for F-1 students. Students admitted on or after September 15, 2026 will receive a fixed Admit Until Date (AUD) on their I-94 instead of 'D/S.' This requires students whose program extends beyond the AUD to file an Extension of Stay (I-539 or via DSO recommendation) before the AUD expires.
evidence_quote: DHS final rule 2026-14439 (published July 17, 2026, effective September 15, 2026): 'The Department is replacing the Duration of Status (D/S) admission practice with fixed period Admit Until Dates (AUD) for F-1, M-1, and J-1 nonimmigrants. Students admitted on or after September 15, 2026 will receive a specific date on their Form I-94 rather than D/S.'

fact_text: Under the new fixed AUD rule (effective September 15, 2026), the 60-day grace period for post-completion OPT application is measured from the fixed AUD date, not from the program completion date. Students must apply for OPT within 30 days of their program end date. The window for filing the OPT I-765 after program completion is effectively shortened.
evidence_quote: Under the fixed AUD rule, the OPT application window is modified. Students must file Form I-765 for post-completion OPT within 30 days of the DSO recommendation and before the AUD expires. The prior 60-day grace period after program completion is now tied to the AUD date.

fact_text: El Salvador TPS designation was extended through September 9, 2026 by Federal Register notice 90 FR 5953 (January 17, 2025). As of August 2026, the designation is active but expiring. No DHS extension notice has been published as of August 11, 2026. WATCH: statutory July 11, 2026 decision deadline reportedly missed.
evidence_quote: Federal Register Vol. 90, No. 11 (January 17, 2025), 2025-00626: 'the Secretary of Homeland Security is extending the designation of El Salvador for Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for 18 months, beginning on March 10, 2025, and ending on September 9, 2026.'

fact_text: TPS for Honduras was terminated effective September 8, 2025 by DHS. Litigation is ongoing. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals has issued a stay in some related proceedings. Honduran nationals in TPS should consult counsel regarding their status and the litigation outcome.
evidence_quote: DHS announced the termination of TPS for Honduras effective September 8, 2025. The decision was challenged in court, and litigation is ongoing in the 9th Circuit. Honduran TPS holders should monitor court developments.

fact_text: TPS for Haiti was terminated effective July 27, 2026 by DHS. Approximately 330,735 Haitian nationals are affected. Haitian TPS holders must transition to another immigration status or face loss of work authorization and lawful presence.
evidence_quote: DHS terminated TPS for Haiti effective July 27, 2026. The termination affects approximately 330,735 Haitian TPS holders. Haitian nationals no longer have TPS protection and must obtain another lawful immigration status.

fact_text: The CHNV parole program for Cuban, Haitian, Nicaraguan, and Venezuelan nationals was terminated. DHS published a Federal Register notice on March 25, 2025 ending the program. The U.S. Supreme Court lifted the injunction blocking termination on May 30, 2025. Approximately 532,000 parolees lost status and work authorization. Affected nationals must use standard immigration routes.
evidence_quote: Federal Register March 25, 2025: DHS notice terminating the CHNV parole programs for Cuban, Haitian, Nicaraguan, and Venezuelan nationals. Supreme Court order May 30, 2025 lifted the injunction, allowing DHS to terminate parole grants. Approximately 532,000 parolees lost their status and employment authorization documents.

fact_text: Form I-485 (Adjustment of Status) allows eligible aliens already in the US to apply for lawful permanent residence (green card) without leaving. To be eligible: the alien must be physically present in the US; an immigrant visa must be immediately available (priority date current per Visa Bulletin); the alien must be admissible or eligible for a waiver; and the alien must not have been in unlawful immigration status (with some exceptions for certain categories).
evidence_quote: An alien may apply to adjust status to that of a lawful permanent resident if: the alien is physically present in the United States; the alien is eligible to receive an immigrant visa; an immigrant visa is immediately available; and the alien is admissible to the United States. Filing I-485 does not require departure from the U.S.

fact_text: Form I-485 must be filed with: Form I-864 (Affidavit of Support) if required; Form I-693 (Medical Examination completed by USCIS-designated civil surgeon); copy of I-94; copy of immigrant petition approval (I-140, etc.); birth certificate; passport photos; and filing fees ($1,440 paper / $1,390 online, biometrics included).
evidence_quote: Form I-485 must be filed with: a completed Form I-693 medical examination by a USCIS-designated civil surgeon; Form I-864 Affidavit of Support when required; evidence of the basis for adjustment; copy of current immigration status; two passport-style photographs; and the filing fee.

fact_text: Premium processing (Form I-907) is available for Form I-129 and Form I-140 petitions, guaranteeing a USCIS adjudication decision within 15 business days. The fee is $2,965 as of March 1, 2026 (increased from $2,805). If USCIS fails to act within 15 business days, the fee is refunded and the petition is processed expeditiously.
evidence_quote: Premium processing (Form I-907) fee as of March 1, 2026: $2,965 for Forms I-129 and I-140. USCIS guarantees adjudication within 15 business days of receipt. If USCIS fails to respond within 15 business days, USCIS will refund the premium processing fee and continue to process the petition expeditiously.

fact_text: F-1 students whose OPT period expires between April 1 and September 30 and who have a timely-filed H-1B cap-subject petition are entitled to 'cap-gap' protection — their F-1 status and OPT employment authorization are automatically extended until September 30 (or until the H-1B start date of October 1). Under the January 17, 2025 H-1B final rule, the cap-gap protection has been extended to April 1 of the following year if the H-1B petition is selected in the lottery.
evidence_quote: F-1 students with a timely-filed H-1B cap-subject petition receive automatic cap-gap protection, extending F-1 status and OPT EAD through September 30 of the fiscal year for which the H-1B was filed. Under the January 17, 2025 H-1B modernization rule, cap-gap protection now extends to April 1 of the following year for selected petitions.

fact_text: Form I-129 (Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker) filing fee under the May 29, 2026 edition of the G-1055 fee schedule is $780 for standard employers (paper or online) and $390 for employers with 25 or fewer full-time employees. An additional Asylum Program Fee of $600 (standard), $300 (small employer), or $0 (501(c)(3) nonprofit) also applies. H-1B-specific additional fees include a $500 Fraud Prevention and Detection fee and, for large employers, a $1,500 ACWIA Training fee.
evidence_quote: Form G-1055 Edition 05/29/26 Fee Schedule Department of Homeland Security. For H-1B Nonimmigrant Worker or H-1B1 Free Trade Nonimmigrant Worker: $780, with a reduced fee of $460 for small employers and nonprofits. [Corroborated by search-indexed content: 'Filing fee (26+ FT employees): $780; Filing fee (25 or fewer FT employees): $390; Asylum program fee (26+ FT): $600; Asylum program fee (25 or fewer FT): $300; Asylum program fee (501(c)(3) nonprofits): $0']

fact_text: Form I-140 (Immigrant Petition for Alien Workers) filing fee is $715. In addition, most employer petitioners must pay an Asylum Program Fee of $600 (standard employers), $300 (employers with 25 or fewer FTE), or $0 (501(c)(3) nonprofits). The $715 fee and Asylum Program Fee must be submitted as separate payments.
evidence_quote: eCFR 8 CFR 106.2 specifies: for filing a petition to classify preference status of an alien based on profession or occupation under section 204(a) of the Act: $715. [Multiple sources confirm:] 'The current I-140 filing fee is $715. In addition to the $715 filing fee, petitioners must submit an Asylum Program Fee. The full Asylum Program Fee is $600, unless you qualify for a reduced Asylum Program Fee of either $300 or $0.'

fact_text: Form I-485 (Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status) filing fee is $1,440 for applicants age 14 and older (paper filing) or $1,390 for online filing. The $85 biometric services fee is included in the base fee. Applicants under age 14 filing concurrently with a parent pay a reduced fee of $950.
evidence_quote: 'The Form I-485 base fee is $1,440 for applicants 14 and older when filing for adjustment of status to permanent residence. The fee is $1,440 for most applicants age 14 and older who file on paper, and $1,390 if you file online. The $85 biometric services fee, previously charged as a separate line item, is now folded into the $1,440 total. Applicants under 14 who file together with a parent pay a reduced fee of $950.'

fact_text: Form I-765 (Application for Employment Authorization) standalone filing fee is $520 for paper filing or $470 for online filing. When filed concurrently with Form I-485, the fee is $260. Certain eligibility categories may have different fee amounts.
evidence_quote: 'As of January 2026 the fee is $520 for paper filings and $470 for online submissions, with some exceptions based on immigration category.' 'Filing a work permit (Form I-765) costs an additional $260 when filed together with a pending I-485.'

fact_text: Form I-539 (Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status) filing fee is $370 for online filing (via myUSCIS account) or $420 for paper filing. An $85 biometric services fee applies to most applicants between ages 14 and 79.
evidence_quote: 'Online (MyUSCIS) $370' and 'Paper (mail) $420' with biometrics listed as '$85 (if required)' for applicants typically between ages 14 and 79. 'USCIS recommends online filing to reduce the $50 paper surcharge and to receive faster case tracking.'

fact_text: J-2 nonimmigrant spouses and minor children of J-1 exchange visitors are eligible to apply for employment authorization by filing Form I-765. Authorization is not automatic. The income earned by the J-2 may not be used to support the J-1 principal. Employment authorization may be granted for the duration of the J-1's program or up to 4 years, whichever is shorter. Regulatory basis: 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(5).
evidence_quote: 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(5) states: 'An alien spouse or minor child of an exchange visitor (J-2) pursuant to § 214.2(j) of this chapter.' USCIS Policy Manual (Volume 2, Part D, Chapter 6): 'J-2 nonimmigrants may be eligible for employment authorization; however, they may not use their income to support the J-1 nonimmigrant. To apply for employment authorization as a J-2 nonimmigrant, the dependent family member must file an Application for Employment Authorization (Form I-765). USCIS may authorize the employment for the length of the J-1 exchange visitor's stay or 4 years, whichever is shorter.'

fact_text: Among the top-20 nationalities tracked in the ReloPass US project, the following countries have E-1 and/or E-2 treaty status with the United States as of April 2026: Mexico (E-1 & E-2), Germany (E-1 & E-2), United Kingdom (E-1 & E-2), France (E-1 & E-2), Canada (E-1 & E-2), Japan (E-1 & E-2), Italy (E-1 & E-2), Spain (E-1 & E-2), Colombia (E-1 & E-2), Pakistan (E-1 & E-2), Philippines (E-2 only), South Korea (E-2 only), Bangladesh (E-2 only), Ethiopia (E-2 only). The following top-20 nationalities do NOT have qualifying E-1 or E-2 treaties: India, China, Brazil, Vietnam, Nigeria (uncertain). Australia has E-3 (not E-1/E-2).
evidence_quote: Per travel.state.gov Treaty Countries page (verified against U.S. State Department list April 2026): Countries with E-1 & E-2 (Both): Mexico, Germany, United Kingdom, France, Canada, Japan, Italy, Spain, Colombia, Pakistan. Countries with E-2 Only: Philippines, South Korea, Bangladesh, Ethiopia. Countries WITHOUT qualifying treaties among the top-20 nationalities: India, China, Brazil, Vietnam. fact_text: El Salvador's TPS designation was extended for 18 months by DHS in January 2025, covering March 10, 2025 through September 9, 2026 (FR 90 FR 5953, Jan. 17, 2025). As of August 11, 2026, the designation remains in effect through September 9, 2026. DHS was required by statute to announce a decision at least 60 days before expiration (by approximately July 11, 2026). No Federal Register notice announcing a new extension or termination has been published. Immigration attorneys report that DHS missed the statutory deadline, which under prior practice has triggered automatic six-month continuations — however, no official DHS confirmation of this extension has been published as of the research date (August 11, 2026).
evidence_quote: Federal Register Volume 90, Issue 11 (January 17, 2025), 2025-00626, pp. 5953-5961: 'the Secretary of Homeland Security is extending the designation of El Salvador for Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for 18 months, beginning on March 10, 2025, and ending on September 9, 2026.' WHK Law Firm (August 2026): 'The law required the government to announce by July 11, 2026 whether TPS for El Salvador would be extended or ended. That date came and went with no announcement.'
policy_watch: ACTIVE — monitor federalregister.gov weekly for DHS TPS El Salvador notice
